title_original: The Brazenness of Bangkok’s Street Youth
excerpt_original: In the portraits of Chardchakaj Waikawee, Thailand's marginalized youth astonish with sheer presence. L’article The Brazenness of Bangkok’s Street Youth est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: The photography of Chardchakaj Waikawee, born in Bangkok in 1980, resists easy classification. It belongs neither to social documentary, with its cool rigor, nor to art portraiture, with its aestheticizing restraint. It is something else, something harder to name, and therefore more precious. His work has traveled internationally for more than fifteen years. “Youth”, the exhibition devoted to him by London’s Graces Mews, brings together a body of analog photographs taken between 2008 and 2020.

The title borrows the Thai phrase wai run , a term that reaches far beyond its literal translation to describe an inner disposition, an energy of being that neither age nor poverty can extinguish. Waikawee’s subjects include motorcycle-taxi drivers, street vendors, and more broadly the young people who survive on the margins of Bangkok’s economy. “Bangkok is chaos,” he says. “Heaven and hell exist on the same street.”

One enters the exhibition through a filmed portrait of the photographer, his voice continuing to murmur through the galleries like an undertow. This sonic device anchors the images in a meditation on memory, time and value: sober words for photographs that are anything but. For Waikawee’s eye plays as much as it bears witness. One need only look at the boy sipping Coca-Cola from a plastic bag, staring straight into the lens with quiet defiance, to be convinced of it. Or the punk whose extravagant pink mohawk bursts through the open sunroof of a champagne-colored Mercedes.

What strikes one, technically, is the deliberate insolence of the process. Waikawee works with expired film, repaired cameras, hand-printing techniques. Cross-processing produces unpredictable chromatic shifts — lemon yellow, scorched orange, acid magenta — which the photographer treats as so many traces of time’s passage upon the material itself. The scratches, the dust, the chemical marks are not accidents but the visible memory of the making, a reminder that every image is also a physical object.

Full of life, these portraits are anything but miserabilist. “Each image reflects a relationship before it becomes a photograph,” Waikawee notes. He foregrounds the personality, the friendship, the singular sense of style of his subjects, who wear their appearance as armor against the social and economic invisibility the city imposes upon them.

Take the laborers crammed into the back of a truck, riding home at night in a tableau at once baroque and entirely ordinary. Or the boy whose back, tattooed with sacred Sak Yant script, is covered in inscriptions down to the waistband of his jeans. One will long remember, too, the doll-like face of the young woman, her eyes lined in black, holding the camera’s gaze without flinching. So many ways, for this sidelined but defiant youth, to compose, with whatever means are to hand, a presence in the world.
“Youth” , by Chardchakaj Waikawee, runs until 19 September 2026 at Graces Mews , London.
